name: Canonical calibration
short: The whole predicted probability vector is correct: among all inputs where the model outputs vector q, the class frequencies are exactly q.
formal: P(Y = k | p̂(X) = q) = q_k   for all k ∈ {1..K} and all q ∈ Δ^K
plain: The strictest notion that is still defined in terms of the model's output alone. It conditions on the entire simplex vector, so nothing about the prediction is thrown away. Every weaker multiclass notion below is obtained by first mapping q through some summary function (max, coordinate k, a group indicator) and asking for calibration of that summary.
useWhen: Downstream code consumes the full probability vector (cost-sensitive decisions with a general loss matrix, probabilistic fusion, belief propagation).
K is small (2-4) and you have plenty of validation data.
You are writing a paper and want to be explicit that the weaker notions are not what you mean.
watchOut: Sample complexity grows exponentially in K. Verifying it directly becomes infeasible at roughly K = 4-5 classes.
Binning in K-1 dimensions is hopeless; use kernel estimators (KCE/SKCE) or KDE-based estimators instead.
Papers say 'strong calibration' for this in the ML literature and for covariate-conditional calibration in the clinical literature. Always check which one is meant.

refs.cite: Vaicenavicius et al., Evaluating model calibration in classification (AISTATS 2019)
Kull et al., Beyond temperature scaling / Dirichlet calibration (NeurIPS 2019)
Silva Filho et al., Classifier calibration: a survey (MLJ 2023)

name: Confidence calibration
short: Only the largest predicted probability has to be right: among predictions made with 70% confidence, 70% are correct.
formal: P(Y = argmax p̂(X) | max p̂(X) = c) = c   for all c ∈ [1/K, 1]
plain: The notion behind 'On Calibration of Modern Neural Networks' and behind almost every reported ECE number. It reduces the prediction to a single scalar, which makes it cheap to estimate and easy to plot, and correspondingly weak: it says nothing about the runner-up classes, and nothing about which class was predicted.
useWhen: The downstream decision only uses accept/reject on the top-1 answer: selective prediction, abstention, routing to a human, OOD triage, active learning.
You need a number that reviewers will recognise without explanation.
K is large and any stronger notion is unestimable with your validation set.
watchOut: A model can be perfectly confidence-calibrated while every individual class is badly miscalibrated: the errors cancel in the aggregate.
It is a strictly weaker condition than class-wise or canonical calibration; do not report it and then claim 'the model is calibrated'.
With many classes, the max-probability distribution is heavily skewed, so equal-width binning puts nearly all the mass in the last bin.

refs.cite: Guo et al., On Calibration of Modern Neural Networks (ICML 2017)
Naeini et al., Obtaining well calibrated probabilities using Bayesian binning (AAAI 2015)

name: Top-label calibration
short: Confidence calibration, but conditioned on which class was predicted, not just on how confident the model was.
formal: P(Y = ĉ(X) | ĉ(X) = k, max p̂(X) = c) = c   for all k, c,   where ĉ = argmax p̂
plain: Fixes the main blind spot of confidence calibration: '90% confident' can mean something different when the model says 'cat' than when it says 'lynx'. Conditioning on the predicted label keeps the estimation problem one-dimensional per class, so it stays practical, while being strictly stronger than confidence calibration.
useWhen: You act on the top-1 prediction but the classes differ in frequency, cost, or difficulty.
You want a strengthening of standard ECE that still fits in your validation budget.
watchOut: Needs enough validation examples per predicted class; rare classes get noisy estimates.
Still ignores the shape of the rest of the vector.

refs.cite: Gupta & Ramdas, Top-label calibration and multiclass-to-binary reductions (ICLR 2022)

name: Class-wise calibration
short: Each coordinate of the probability vector is calibrated on its own, as if it were a binary problem.
formal: P(Y = k | p̂_k(X) = q) = q   for every class k and every q ∈ [0,1]
plain: Treats the K-class problem as K one-vs-rest binary problems and asks each to be calibrated. Much cheaper to estimate than canonical calibration (K one-dimensional problems instead of one K-dimensional one) while retaining per-class meaning. It does not imply canonical calibration: the coordinates can be individually right and jointly wrong.
useWhen: You use per-class probabilities independently: multi-label style thresholding, per-class alerting, screening for one specific class.
Class imbalance matters and you want to see which classes are overconfident.
You want a defensible middle ground between confidence and canonical calibration.
watchOut: For large K, most p̂_k are near zero and class-wise ECE is dominated by the near-zero region; report it per class or use equal-mass bins.
Being class-wise calibrated for all k does not make the vector jointly calibrated.

refs.cite: Zadrozny & Elkan, Transforming classifier scores into accurate multiclass probability estimates (KDD 2002)
Kull et al., Beyond temperature scaling (NeurIPS 2019)
Kumar et al., Verified uncertainty calibration (NeurIPS 2019)

name: Class-aggregated calibration
short: Pool all K predicted probabilities from all examples into one pile and require that pile to be calibrated.
formal: P(Y = k | p̂_k(X) = q, over the pooled set of all (k, q) pairs) = q
plain: A single-number summary that uses every entry of the probability vector rather than only the max. It is neither stronger nor weaker than confidence calibration; it is a different projection. Popularised as the estimand behind the Static Calibration Error, and used in generalisation-gap work under the name class-aggregated calibration error.
useWhen: You want one number that is sensitive to the whole vector but cheaper than canonical calibration.
Comparing models where the tail of the probability vector matters.
watchOut: Pooling hides which class is responsible for the error. Pair it with a per-class breakdown.
Dominated by the many near-zero entries when K is large.

refs.cite: Nixon et al., Measuring calibration in deep learning (CVPR-W 2019)
Jiang et al., Assessing generalization of SGD via disagreement (ICLR 2022)

name: Mean calibration
short: The average predicted probability equals the observed event rate. The weakest useful requirement.
plain: Level 1 of the clinical calibration hierarchy. It only checks the overall level, so a model that is wildly overconfident on half the data and underconfident on the other half passes. Still worth reporting first, because failing it usually means a prevalence shift between development and deployment populations, which is a different problem from a badly shaped calibration curve.
useWhen: First diagnostic on any external validation set.
Monitoring for prevalence/base-rate drift in production.
Very small validation sets, where nothing more refined can be estimated.
watchOut: Passing it says almost nothing. Never report it alone.
It is fixed trivially by an intercept correction, which does not fix the shape of the curve.

refs.cite: Van Calster et al., A calibration hierarchy for risk models (J Clin Epi 2016)
Van Calster et al., Calibration: the Achilles heel of predictive analytics (BMC Med 2019)

name: Weak calibration (slope & intercept)
short: Regress the outcome on the logit of the prediction: the intercept should be 0 and the slope should be 1.
formal: In  logit P(Y=1|X) = a + b · logit p̂(X),  weak calibration holds iff a = 0 and b = 1
plain: Level 2 of the clinical hierarchy. The slope measures whether predictions are too extreme (b < 1, the classic overfitting signature) or too moderate (b > 1); the intercept measures the level. Two interpretable numbers with confidence intervals, which is why it dominates the medical prediction-model literature.
useWhen: External validation of a risk model, where you must report interpretable, testable numbers.
Detecting overfitting during internal validation (slope < 1).
Small validation sets, where a flexible calibration curve would be unstable.
watchOut: Assumes the miscalibration is a logistic-linear distortion. A U-shaped calibration curve can average out to slope 1, intercept 0.
Slope and intercept must be interpreted jointly, never separately.

refs.cite: Van Calster et al., A calibration hierarchy for risk models (J Clin Epi 2016)
Steyerberg, Clinical Prediction Models (Springer)

name: Moderate calibration
short: Among everyone given a predicted risk of R%, the event rate is R%. This is what most people mean by 'calibrated'.
formal: P(Y = 1 | p̂(X) = q) = q   for all q ∈ [0,1]
plain: Level 3 of the clinical hierarchy, and identical to canonical calibration in the binary case. Van Calster et al. prove that moderate calibration is sufficient for non-harmful decision making at any decision threshold, which is a strong practical argument for treating it, rather than anything stricter, as the target.
useWhen: Binary risk prediction where a threshold will be applied and the threshold may change.
You want the strongest notion that is actually achievable and verifiable.
Default target for any binary probabilistic model.
watchOut: Assessment needs a flexible curve (loess/spline), not 10 bins; binned estimates are unstable on small validation sets.
A diagonal calibration curve does not imply strong (covariate-conditional) calibration.

refs.cite: Van Calster et al., A calibration hierarchy for risk models (J Clin Epi 2016)
Van Calster & Vickers, Calibration of risk prediction models: impact on decision-analytic performance (Med Decis Making 2015)

name: Strong (covariate-conditional) calibration
short: The prediction is correct for every covariate pattern, i.e. the model has recovered the true conditional probability.
formal: p̂(x) = P(Y = 1 | X = x)   for every x
plain: Level 4 of the clinical hierarchy, and the point at which calibration stops being a property of the output distribution and becomes a claim of having solved the problem. Van Calster et al. argue it is unrealistic and even counterproductive as a target, because chasing it encourages overly complex models; the ML fairness literature reaches for multicalibration as the tractable relaxation instead.
useWhen: As a theoretical reference point in a proof or a definition section.
Rarely as an empirical target.
watchOut: Unverifiable from data: you never see repeated draws at a single x.
'Strong calibration' in the ML literature (Vaicenavicius, Widmann) usually means canonical calibration, which is much weaker than this. Different field, same words.

refs.cite: Van Calster et al., A calibration hierarchy for risk models (J Clin Epi 2016)

name: Group-wise calibration
short: Calibration holds separately inside each of a small, pre-specified set of groups.
formal: P(Y = 1 | p̂(X) = q, G(X) = g) = q   for all q and all g in a fixed group set G
plain: The fairness-motivated first step beyond global calibration: a model calibrated overall can be systematically overconfident for one demographic group and underconfident for another. The groups must be named in advance and observable at evaluation time, which is both its practicality and its limitation.
useWhen: Regulated or high-stakes settings with legally protected attributes.
Deployment across sites, devices, sensors, or seasons: treat each as a group.
You have enough data per group to estimate a curve.
watchOut: Only protects the groups you thought of; intersections and unnamed subpopulations remain exposed. That is exactly the gap multicalibration closes.
Groups may not be available at inference time, which rules out simply fitting a separate calibrator per group.
Calibration within groups can conflict with equalised error rates; the impossibility results apply.

refs.cite: Kleinberg et al., Inherent trade-offs in the fair determination of risk scores (ITCS 2017)
Pleiss et al., On fairness and calibration (NeurIPS 2017)

name: Multicalibration
short: Calibration holds simultaneously on every subpopulation that can be picked out by some rich class of functions, not just a handful of named groups.
formal: For all g ∈ C:  E[ Y − p̂(X) | p̂(X) = v, g(X) = 1 ] ≈ 0   for all v
plain: Conditions on level sets and group membership at once, over an entire computationally-identifiable class of groups including overlaps and intersections. Standard calibration is the special case C = {everything}. Remarkably, it is achievable by post-processing with a boosting-style algorithm, and it does not degrade accuracy, which is unusual among fairness constraints.
useWhen: Fairness requirements that must cover intersectional and unanticipated subgroups.
Distribution shift robustness: multicalibrated predictors transfer better across subpopulations.
Confidence scoring for LLMs, where the useful 'groups' are functions of the prompt or the internal representation.
watchOut: You still choose the class C. Richer C means stronger guarantee and more data needed.
Several inequivalent versions exist (ℓ∞, ℓ1, ℓ2, low-degree, smooth). State which one you use.
Multiaccuracy is the weaker sibling and is often what an algorithm actually delivers.

refs.cite: Hébert-Johnson et al., Multicalibration: calibration for the (computationally-identifiable) masses (ICML 2018)
Gopalan et al., Low-degree multicalibration (COLT 2022)
Detommaso et al., Multicalibration for confidence scoring in LLMs (ICML 2024)

name: Multiaccuracy
short: Predictions are unbiased on every group in a class, but not necessarily calibrated within each group.
formal: For all g ∈ C:  E[ (Y − p̂(X)) · g(X) ] ≈ 0
plain: Drops the conditioning on the level set. The average residual on each group is zero, which rules out systematic under-prediction of a subpopulation, but the group's calibration curve can still be badly shaped. Cheaper to audit and to achieve than multicalibration, and often enough for bias auditing.
useWhen: Bias auditing where the concern is systematic under/over-prediction for a group.
You want the multi-group guarantee at a fraction of the sample cost.
watchOut: Weaker than multicalibration: errors can cancel across the score range within a group.

refs.cite: Kim, Ghorbani & Zou, Multiaccuracy: black-box post-processing for fairness (AIES 2019)

name: Adversarial group calibration
short: Calibration must survive the worst subset of the data of a given size, found adversarially.
formal: For every measurable S ⊆ X with P(S) ≥ δ, the forecaster is (approximately) calibrated conditional on X ∈ S
plain: The regression analogue of multicalibration, stated as a worst-case over slices rather than over a function class. In practice it is estimated by repeatedly sampling random subsets of increasing size and reporting the maximum calibration error observed, which makes it one of the few multi-group notions with an out-of-the-box implementation.
useWhen: Regression or UQ models where average calibration looks fine but you suspect it is masking local failures.
Model-based control and scientific ML, where the deployment slice is not the training slice.
watchOut: The random-subset estimator is a lower bound on the true worst case.
Sensitive to the minimum group size δ; report it.

refs.cite: Zhao, Ma & Ermon, Individual calibration with randomized forecasting (ICML 2020)
Chung et al., Uncertainty Toolbox (2021)

name: Decision calibration
short: For every decision rule in a chosen class, the loss you predict is the loss you get.
formal: For all loss functions ℓ in a class L and the induced Bayes actions δ_ℓ:  E[ ℓ(δ_ℓ(p̂), Y) ] = E_p̂[ ℓ(δ_ℓ(p̂), Ŷ) ]
plain: Re-frames calibration around what the probabilities are for. Instead of asking the vector to be right in the abstract, it asks that any downstream decision maker drawn from a specified class cannot tell the difference between the predicted distribution and reality, in terms of realised loss. Sits between confidence and canonical calibration, and the class L controls exactly where.
useWhen: The probability vector feeds a known family of decisions with known costs (triage, inventory, treatment choice).
K is large enough that canonical calibration is out of reach, but confidence calibration is clearly insufficient.
You want a guarantee you can state in terms of regret, not in terms of bins.
watchOut: You must specify the decision class up front; guarantees do not extend beyond it.
Newer and less tooled than ECE-style notions.

refs.cite: Zhao et al., Calibrating predictions to decisions (NeurIPS 2021)
Dwork et al., Outcome indistinguishability (STOC 2021)

name: F-calibration
short: A meta-notion: pick a class of test functions, and require the residual to be uncorrelated with every function in it.
formal: E[ (e_Y − p̂(X)) · f(p̂(X)) ] = 0   for all f ∈ F   (and the analogous form for general target spaces)
plain: The organising principle behind most of the notions on this page. Confidence, class-wise and canonical calibration are all recovered by choosing F appropriately, as are the regression notions and multicalibration. Choosing F to be a reproducing-kernel Hilbert space unit ball turns the calibration error into an MMD, which gives unbiased estimators and genuine hypothesis tests instead of bin-count-dependent point estimates.
useWhen: Writing a definitions section and wanting one framework instead of a list.
You need a statistical test of calibration with a controlled type-I error rate.
Structured or non-standard output spaces where no named notion exists yet.
watchOut: Kernel and bandwidth choice matters, and the resulting numbers are not comparable across choices.
The U-statistic estimator of the squared kernel error can be negative; use it as a test statistic, not as a reported error.

refs.cite: Widmann, Lindsten & Zachariah, Calibration tests in multi-class classification (NeurIPS 2019)
Widmann et al., Calibration tests beyond classification (ICLR 2021)
Glaser et al., Fast and scalable score-based kernel calibration tests (UAI 2023)

name: Smooth calibration & distance to calibration
short: How far is this predictor, in L1, from the nearest perfectly calibrated one? Test functions are Lipschitz rather than arbitrary.
formal: dCE(f) = inf over perfectly calibrated g of E|f(X) − g(X)|;   smCE(f) = sup over 1-Lipschitz η of E[(Y − f(X)) η(f(X))]
plain: A response to a real problem: ECE is discontinuous in the predictor, so a model that is intuitively almost calibrated can have large ECE, and ECE cannot be estimated consistently. Distance-to-calibration is proposed as the ground-truth quantity, and smooth calibration error is a tractable measure provably within constant factors of it. This is the notion to cite when someone objects that your ECE is an artefact of binning.
useWhen: You need a calibration number that is robust to binning choices and to tiny perturbations of the predictor.
Comparing or ranking many models by reliability.
Theory work where ECE's pathologies are the point.
watchOut: Computing the exact calibration distance is NP-hard in general; use smECE as the practical surrogate.
Currently binary/scalar-score oriented; the multiclass story is less developed.

refs.cite: Błasiok, Gopalan, Hu & Nakkiran, A unifying theory of distance from calibration (STOC 2023)
Błasiok & Nakkiran, Smooth ECE: principled reliability diagrams via kernel smoothing (ICLR 2024)
Kakade & Foster, Deterministic calibration and Nash equilibrium (2008)

name: Quantile calibration
short: The predicted p-quantile is exceeded a fraction p of the time, averaged over the whole dataset.
formal: P( Y ≤ F̂_X^{-1}(p) ) = p   for all p ∈ [0,1],   equivalently  PIT = F̂_X(Y) ~ Uniform(0,1)
plain: The default notion in regression UQ and the one behind every 'my 90% interval covers 90% of the test points' claim. It is a marginal statement: the coverage is averaged over inputs, so a forecaster can be quantile-calibrated while being far too wide on easy points and far too narrow on hard ones. Cheap to check with a PIT histogram.
useWhen: Reporting interval coverage for a regression or forecasting model.
Post-hoc recalibration with a monotone CDF transform, which targets exactly this notion.
You need something checkable with a few hundred validation points.
watchOut: Averaging hides input-dependent failure. Always pair with sharpness and, if you can, adversarial group calibration.
Achievable trivially by predicting the marginal distribution of Y for every input.
Called 'probabilistic calibration' by Gneiting et al. and just 'calibration' by many ML papers.

refs.cite: Kuleshov, Fenner & Ermon, Accurate uncertainties for deep learning using calibrated regression (ICML 2018)
Gneiting, Balabdaoui & Raftery, Probabilistic forecasts, calibration and sharpness (JRSS-B 2007)

name: Distribution calibration (regression)
short: Among all inputs where the model predicts the same distribution F, the outcomes really are distributed as F.
formal: P( Y = y | F̂_X = F ) = f(y)   for all y and all predicted distributions F
plain: The regression counterpart of canonical calibration, and strictly stronger than quantile calibration. If the model says N(20, 3) on some set of days, the observed values on those days should look like N(20, 3), not merely have the right average coverage. Conditioning on the full predicted distribution makes it hard to satisfy or verify exactly.
useWhen: Heteroscedastic problems where per-input distribution shape is the point.
Downstream sampling or simulation from the predictive distribution.
You need to justify why quantile calibration is not enough for your application.
watchOut: Widely described as unattainable exactly in practice; treat it as a direction, not a pass/fail test.
Estimation requires smoothing over the space of predicted distributions.

refs.cite: Song, Diethe, Kull & Flach, Distribution calibration for regression (ICML 2019)

name: Variance calibration
short: The predicted variance matches the actual squared error, at every level of predicted variance.
formal: E[ (Y − μ̂(X))² | σ̂²(X) = σ² ] = σ²   for all σ²
plain: Designed for models that emit a mean and a variance rather than a full CDF, which covers most deep heteroscedastic regressors and ensembles. Conditions on the predicted uncertainty level, so it catches the common failure where a network's error bars are uniformly too small. For an unbiased model it coincides with distribution calibration.
useWhen: Gaussian-output networks, deep ensembles, MC dropout, evidential regression.
Physical-science and engineering models where the error bar is the deliverable.
You want a per-uncertainty-level diagnostic rather than a marginal coverage number.
watchOut: Assumes a parametric (usually Gaussian) predictive distribution.
Binning is over σ̂, so it inherits all the usual bin-count sensitivity; ENCE is not comparable across binning schemes.
Confounded by bias in μ̂: a biased mean inflates the observed error.

refs.cite: Levi et al., Evaluating and calibrating uncertainty prediction in regression tasks (Sensors 2022)
Laves et al., Well-calibrated regression uncertainty in medical imaging with deep learning (MIDL 2020)
Küppers et al., Parametric and multivariate uncertainty calibration (ECCV-W 2022)

name: Threshold calibration
short: Quantile calibration must hold within every group of inputs that a threshold decision would treat the same way.
formal: Quantile calibration holds conditional on the event { F̂_X(y₀) ≤ α },  for all thresholds y₀ and levels α
plain: Sits strictly between quantile and distribution calibration, and was constructed to fix a concrete problem: quantile calibration is not preserved under the conditioning that a threshold-based decision maker induces, so an average-calibrated forecast can be badly miscalibrated on exactly the subset that triggers an action.
useWhen: Alerting and screening on a continuous quantity ('flag if predicted load exceeds L').
You want a stronger-than-marginal guarantee that is still achievable, unlike distribution calibration.
watchOut: Less tooling than quantile calibration; expect to implement the diagnostic yourself.

refs.cite: Sahoo, Zhao & Ermon, Reliable decisions with threshold calibration (NeurIPS 2021)

name: Individual calibration
short: The quantile claim is correct for each single input, not on average over inputs.
formal: P( Y ≤ F̂_x^{-1}(p) | X = x ) = p   for every x and every p
plain: The regression version of covariate-conditional calibration, and the honest answer to 'but is my 90% interval 90% for *this* patient?'. It is provably impossible to verify, and impossible to achieve with a deterministic forecaster; the workable version is a randomized forecaster that is individually calibrated with high probability over its own randomness.
useWhen: Stating what your method does not provide.
Applications where per-instance guarantees are genuinely required and randomized forecasts are acceptable.
watchOut: Deterministic models cannot achieve it; claims to the contrary are usually about average calibration.
Not testable from data.

refs.cite: Zhao, Ma & Ermon, Individual calibration with randomized forecasting (ICML 2020)
Barber et al., The limits of distribution-free conditional predictive inference (2019)

name: Parity calibration
short: The probability the model implies for 'the next value goes up' should match how often it actually goes up.
formal: P( Y_t > Y_{t−1} | p̂_t^parity = q ) = q,  where p̂_t^parity is induced by the regression forecast
plain: A worked example of a general lesson: calibration is not preserved when you transform the prediction. A time-series forecaster can be quantile-calibrated on levels and badly miscalibrated on the binary up/down event derived from those levels, which is often the event the user actually cares about.
useWhen: Time series where the user reads the forecast as a direction (clinical monitoring, weather, energy, prices).
Any setting where a binary event is derived from a continuous forecast.
watchOut: Do not assume it follows from regression calibration; it does not.
Recalibrate for the event you will actually report.

refs.cite: Chung et al., Parity calibration (UAI 2023)

name: Semantic calibration (LLMs)
short: The model's confidence in the meaning of an answer, not in its tokens, matches how often that meaning is correct.
formal: P( answer correct | ŝ(semantic cluster) = c ) = c,  where confidence is estimated from repeated samples grouped by semantic equivalence
plain: Token-level calibration is well known for base models but is the wrong unit: the same answer has many surface forms, so token probabilities spread mass over paraphrases. Semantic calibration groups samples into equivalence classes first. Recent work finds base models are surprisingly well calibrated in this sense, and that RLHF and chain-of-thought disrupt it.
useWhen: Open-ended QA and generation, where correctness is a property of meaning.
Hallucination detection and abstention policies.
Comparing base and post-trained models on reliability rather than accuracy.
watchOut: Requires an equivalence/entailment judge, which introduces its own errors.
Sampling cost: you need multiple generations per prompt.
Do not conflate with next-token calibration or with verbalized confidence.

refs.cite: Trained on tokens, calibrated on concepts: the emergence of semantic calibration in LLMs (2025)
Kuhn, Gal & Farquhar, Semantic uncertainty (ICLR 2023)

name: Verbalized-confidence calibration (LLMs)
short: When the model writes '80% sure', it should be right 80% of the time.
formal: P( response correct | verbalized confidence = c ) = c
plain: The only notion available for black-box APIs that do not return logprobs, and the one that matters for a human reading the output. Empirically fragile: RLHF-tuned models are systematically overconfident, and the numbers move substantially with prompt wording, response scale, and aggregation strategy, so the elicitation protocol is part of the measurement.
useWhen: Black-box models, or interfaces where a human reads the confidence.
Agent systems that route on self-reported certainty.
watchOut: Protocol sensitivity: report the exact prompt, the scale, and the sampling strategy, or the number is not reproducible.
Often worse than token-probability baselines for RL-trained models; check both.
Coarse: models cluster on round numbers like 0.8, 0.9, 0.95.

refs.cite: Lin, Hilton & Evans, Teaching models to express their uncertainty in words (TMLR 2022)
Tian et al., Just ask for calibration (EMNLP 2023)
Xiong et al., Can LLMs express their uncertainty? (ICLR 2024)
Geng et al., A survey of confidence estimation and calibration in LLMs (NAACL 2024)

name: Detection calibration
short: An object detector's confidence must match its precision conditioned on where and how big the box is, not just on the score.
formal: P( correct detection | score = s, box = (cx, cy, w, h) ) = s
plain: In detection the score is emitted jointly with a geometry, and miscalibration is typically location- and scale-dependent: small boxes near the image border behave differently from large central ones. Conditioning only on the score averages this away. The same idea extends to the regression side, where the predicted box distribution should be quantile- or variance-calibrated.
useWhen: Object detection and instance segmentation, especially safety-critical perception.
Sensor fusion, where per-detection confidences are combined across modalities.
Tracking, where detection confidence feeds a data-association or filtering step.
watchOut: Requires a matching criterion (IoU threshold) before calibration is even defined; the number depends on it.
Conditioning on several box dimensions multiplies the binning problem; use KDE-based estimators.
Confidence calibration of the class score and calibration of the box regression are separate problems.

refs.cite: Küppers et al., Multivariate confidence calibration for object detection (CVPR-W 2020)
Popordanoska et al., Beyond classification: definition and density-based estimation of calibration in object detection (WACV 2024)

name: Sequential / online calibration
short: Empirical frequencies converge to the forecasts over a stream, with no assumption that the data is i.i.d. or even stochastic.
formal: For every forecast value q:  ( Σ_t 1{p̂_t = q} · y_t ) / ( Σ_t 1{p̂_t = q} ) → q  as t → ∞
plain: The game-theoretic root of the whole topic, predating the ML literature. No distributional assumption at all: the sequence may be chosen adversarially. Deterministic forecasters cannot achieve it, randomized ones can, and the resulting no-regret and equilibrium connections are why calibration is considered a fundamental property rather than a cosmetic one.
useWhen: Streaming and non-stationary deployment, where an i.i.d. validation set does not exist.
Online recalibration with drift.
Theory framing: calibration as a no-regret property.
watchOut: Asymptotic guarantees can have slow rates; check the regret bound, not just the limit.
Requires randomization, which many deployments will not accept.

refs.cite: Dawid, The well-calibrated Bayesian (JASA 1982)
Foster & Vohra, Asymptotic calibration (Biometrika 1998)
Gibbs & Candès, Adaptive conformal inference under distribution shift (NeurIPS 2021)

name: Marginal coverage (conformal)
short: Not calibration. A finite-sample guarantee that a prediction set contains the truth with probability 1−α, averaged over everything.
formal: P( Y ∈ C_α(X) ) ≥ 1 − α,   with probability over both the calibration set and the test point
plain: Included here because it is constantly confused with calibration, and because the conformal literature unhelpfully calls its held-out split the 'calibration set'. Conformal gives you a set with a guaranteed marginal coverage rate and no assumptions beyond exchangeability; it does not give you a probability attached to a specific outcome, and it says nothing conditional on X. Calibration and coverage answer different questions and are worth reporting together.
useWhen: You need a finite-sample, assumption-light guarantee.
The deliverable is a set or interval rather than a probability.
As a complement to a calibration analysis, not a replacement.
watchOut: Marginal, not conditional: coverage can be 99% on easy inputs and 60% on hard ones.
Conditional coverage is impossible distribution-free, which is the same wall that individual calibration hits.
'Calibration set' in conformal papers means 'held-out split', not 'calibrated'.

refs.cite: Angelopoulos & Bates, A gentle introduction to conformal prediction (2021)
Vovk, Gammerman & Shafer, Algorithmic Learning in a Random World

name: Sharpness / refinement
short: Not calibration, but the thing that stops calibration from being trivial: how concentrated the predictions are.
formal: Brier score = calibration loss − refinement (resolution) + irreducible noise;  sharpness = Var(p̂) or the width of the predictive distribution
plain: Predicting the base rate for every input is perfectly calibrated and perfectly useless. Every proper scoring rule decomposes into a calibration term and a refinement/sharpness term, and any honest calibration report shows both. The standard framing is: maximise sharpness subject to calibration.
useWhen: Always. Report alongside any calibration metric.
Diagnosing recalibration methods that improve ECE by flattening predictions toward the base rate.
watchOut: A drop in ECE accompanied by a drop in sharpness is usually not an improvement.
Accuracy alone is not sharpness; a model can be accurate and unsharp.

refs.cite: Gneiting, Balabdaoui & Raftery, Probabilistic forecasts, calibration and sharpness (JRSS-B 2007)
DeGroot & Fienberg, The comparison and evaluation of forecasters (1983)
Kull & Flach, Novel decompositions of proper scoring rules (ECML 2015)

name: Expected Calibration Error (ECE)
short: Bin predictions by confidence, average |accuracy − confidence| weighted by bin size.
formal: ECE = Σ_b (n_b / n) · | acc(b) − conf(b) |
plain: The default. Simple, plottable next to a reliability diagram, and understood by everyone. Also the most criticised estimator in the field: it is biased (usually downward), its value depends on the bin count, it is discontinuous in the predictor, and it is not a consistent estimator of any well-behaved calibration distance.
watchOut: Report the bin count and the binning scheme, always. Numbers across papers with different bin counts are not comparable.
Equal-width bins are near-useless when confidences pile up at 1.0; use equal-mass bins (ACE).
Biased: fewer bins understate the error; more bins increase variance.
A perfectly calibrated model has nonzero measured ECE at finite n.

code.snippet:
from netcal.metrics import ECE
ece = ECE(bins=15).measure(confidences, labels)

from torchmetrics.classification import MulticlassCalibrationError
MulticlassCalibrationError(num_classes=K, n_bins=15, norm='l1')(probs, targets)

from torch_uncertainty.metrics import CalibrationError
CalibrationError(task='multiclass', num_classes=K)(probs, targets)

refs.cite: Naeini et al. (AAAI 2015)
Roelofs et al., Mitigating bias in calibration error estimation (AISTATS 2022)

name: Adaptive ECE / ACE / TACE
short: ECE with equal-count bins instead of equal-width bins, optionally after dropping near-zero probabilities.
formal: Same as ECE, with bin edges at the empirical quantiles of the confidence distribution
plain: The cheapest meaningful fix to standard ECE. Equal-mass bins put estimation effort where the data is, which matters enormously when confidences are concentrated near 1 or, for class-wise variants, near 0. Thresholded ACE additionally ignores probabilities below a cutoff so that the many irrelevant near-zero entries do not dominate.
watchOut: Still binned, so still bin-count dependent, just less pathologically.
The threshold in TACE is an extra reported hyperparameter.

code.snippet:
from netcal.metrics import ACE
ace = ACE(bins=15).measure(confidences, labels)
from torch_uncertainty.metrics import AdaptiveCalibrationError

refs.cite: Nixon et al., Measuring calibration in deep learning (CVPR-W 2019)

name: Maximum Calibration Error (MCE)
short: The largest gap between accuracy and confidence over all bins.
formal: MCE = max_b | acc(b) − conf(b) |
plain: A worst-case companion to ECE, motivated by safety-critical settings where the average error is the wrong summary. In practice it is dominated by the sparsest bin and is very noisy.
watchOut: High variance: usually attained in a bin with a handful of samples. Report bin occupancy alongside.
Use equal-mass bins, or the number is meaningless.

code.snippet:
from netcal.metrics import MCE
mce = MCE(bins=15).measure(confidences, labels)

refs.cite: Naeini et al. (AAAI 2015)

name: Class-wise ECE / Static Calibration Error
short: Run the ECE computation on each class's probability column and average over classes.
formal: cwECE = (1/K) Σ_k Σ_b (n_{b,k}/n) · | freq_k(b) − p̄_k(b) |
plain: The standard estimator for class-wise calibration, and for class-aggregated calibration when the classes are pooled rather than averaged. Far more informative than top-label ECE because you can see which classes are overconfident, at the cost of needing more validation data per class.
watchOut: For large K it is dominated by the near-zero probability region; report per-class values or threshold.
Averaging over classes hides a single badly calibrated rare class; also report the max.

code.snippet:
from netcal.metrics import ECE
# per-class one-vs-rest
ece = ECE(bins=15).measure(probs, labels)  # probs: (n, K)
from torch_uncertainty.metrics import ClasswiseCalibrationError

import calibration as cal
cal.get_calibration_error(probs, labels)  # marginal / top-label variants

refs.cite: Kull et al. (NeurIPS 2019)
Nixon et al. (CVPR-W 2019)

name: Debiased ECE with bootstrap CIs
short: A bias-corrected estimator of the ℓ2 calibration error, plus confidence intervals so you know whether a difference is real.
formal: Debiased estimate of  E[ (E[Y|p̂] − p̂)² ]^{1/2}, with bootstrap resampling for intervals
plain: Addresses the fact that the naive plugin ECE systematically underestimates the true calibration error, so a recalibration method can look better than it is. The same paper introduces scaling-binning, a recalibrator whose calibration error can actually be measured with fewer samples.
watchOut: The ℓ2 version is what is debiased; the ℓ1 (standard ECE) case is harder.
Bootstrap intervals assume an i.i.d. validation set.

code.snippet:
import calibration as cal
err = cal.get_calibration_error(model_probs, labels)
lo, hi = cal.get_calibration_error_uncertainties(model_probs, labels)

refs.cite: Kumar, Liang & Ma, Verified uncertainty calibration (NeurIPS 2019)

name: SmoothECE (smCE)
short: Smooth the residuals with an RBF kernel, then compute ECE of the smoothed function. Hyperparameter-free and provably well-behaved.
formal: smECE_σ(f) = E| (K_σ * residual)(f(X)) |, with an automatically selected bandwidth σ
plain: The practical answer to the binning critique. It is a consistent calibration measure in the sense of the distance-from-calibration theory, meaning it is within constant factors of the true distance to the nearest calibrated predictor, and the associated smoothed reliability diagram visually encodes the number it reports. If you only change one thing about how you measure calibration, change ECE to this.
watchOut: Scalar-score oriented; for multiclass you apply it to a reduction (top-label or per-class).
Fixing the bandwidth manually for comparability costs you some of the theoretical guarantee.

code.snippet:
pip install relplot
import relplot
smece = relplot.smECE(f, y)          # auto bandwidth
relplot.rel_diagram(f, y)             # smoothed reliability diagram
from torch_uncertainty.metrics import SmoothECE

refs.cite: Błasiok & Nakkiran, Smooth ECE (ICLR 2024)
Błasiok et al., A unifying theory of distance from calibration (STOC 2023)

name: KDE-based calibration error
short: Replace hard bins with a kernel density estimate of the conditional accuracy. Consistent and differentiable.
formal: Estimate E[Y | p̂ = q] by a Nadaraya-Watson / Dirichlet-kernel regression on the simplex, then integrate the deviation
plain: The main route to estimating canonical calibration error in more than two classes, where binning is hopeless. Being differentiable, it can also be used as a training-time penalty. Extended to object detection, where the conditioning variable includes box geometry.
watchOut: Bandwidth selection matters and should be reported.
Cost grows with n; subsample or use a fast approximation for large validation sets.

code.snippet:
# reference implementation from the paper
from ece_kde import get_ece_kde
ece = get_ece_kde(probs, labels, bandwidth, p=1, mc_type='canonical')

refs.cite: Popordanoska, Sayer & Blaschko, A consistent and differentiable Lp canonical calibration error estimator (NeurIPS 2022)
Zhang, Kailkhura & Han, Mix-n-Match (ICML 2020)

name: Kernel Calibration Error (KCE / SKCE / MMCE)
short: An MMD between the joint distribution of (prediction, outcome) and what calibration would imply. Comes with a hypothesis test.
formal: SKCE = MMD-type statistic with a matrix-valued kernel; unbiased U-statistic estimator, quadratic in n
plain: The estimator that goes with the F-calibration framework. Unlike ECE it needs no binning, uses the whole probability vector, has an unbiased estimator, and supports a proper test of the null hypothesis that the model is calibrated. MMCE is the earlier top-label-only version, and is differentiable so it doubles as a training regulariser.
watchOut: The unbiased estimator of the squared error can be negative. Use it as a test statistic; do not report it as 'the calibration error'.
Not interpretable in absolute terms and not comparable across kernels or bandwidths.
O(n²) runtime; use the linear-time variants or the score-based test for large n.

code.snippet:
from pycalibration import ca
skce = ca.SKCE(ca.tensor(ca.ExponentialKernel(), ca.WhiteKernel()))
skce(predictions, outcomes)

refs.cite: Widmann, Lindsten & Zachariah (NeurIPS 2019)
Widmann et al., Calibration tests beyond classification (ICLR 2021)
Kumar, Sarawagi & Jain, Trainable calibration measures (ICML 2018)

name: Brier score & its calibration–refinement decomposition
short: A proper scoring rule that splits exactly into a calibration term, a refinement term, and irreducible noise.
formal: BS = E‖p̂ − e_Y‖²  =  calibration loss − resolution + uncertainty
plain: The honest single number: it cannot be gamed by flattening predictions, because doing so destroys the resolution term. The decomposition is the cleanest way to show that a recalibration method improved calibration without costing sharpness, and it is what calibration–sharpness diagrams plot.
watchOut: The decomposition's calibration term needs an estimate of E[Y|p̂], so it inherits binning or smoothing choices.
A better Brier score does not imply better calibration; check the terms separately.

code.snippet:
from sklearn.metrics import brier_score_loss
brier_score_loss(y_true, p_hat)
from netcal.metrics import ECE  # pair with brier for the decomposition

refs.cite: Brier (1950)
Kull & Flach, Novel decompositions of proper scoring rules (ECML 2015)

name: Negative log-likelihood
short: The other standard proper scoring rule. Sensitive to calibration, but conflates it with accuracy.
formal: NLL = −E[ log p̂_Y(X) ]
plain: Worth reporting because it is proper and because temperature scaling is fitted by minimising it, but it is unbounded and dominated by a few confident mistakes, which makes it a poor standalone calibration diagnostic.
watchOut: One confident error can swamp the average.
Improvements can come entirely from accuracy rather than calibration.

code.snippet:
from sklearn.metrics import log_loss
log_loss(y_true, probs)

refs.cite: Gneiting & Raftery, Strictly proper scoring rules (JASA 2007)

name: Calibration slope, intercept & flexible curve (ICI/E50/E90)
short: Two interpretable regression coefficients with confidence intervals, plus a smooth curve and its average absolute deviation from the diagonal.
formal: logit(Y) ~ a + b·logit(p̂);  ICI = mean |ĝ(p̂) − p̂| over the loess/spline curve ĝ
plain: The clinical-prediction toolkit. Slope and intercept test weak calibration; the flexible curve assesses moderate calibration without binning; ICI, E50 and E90 summarise the curve as a mean, median and 90th-percentile absolute deviation. This is what reviewers in medicine and epidemiology expect, and it is better statistics than a 10-bin ECE.
watchOut: Flexible curves are unstable below a few hundred events; the literature warns explicitly about small validation sets.
Report the confidence intervals, not just the point estimates.

code.snippet:
library(CalibrationCurves)
val.prob.ci.2(p_hat, y)   # slope, intercept, ICI, E50, E90, flexible curve

from sklearn.calibration import calibration_curve
prob_true, prob_pred = calibration_curve(y, p_hat, n_bins=10, strategy='quantile')

refs.cite: Van Calster et al. (J Clin Epi 2016)
Austin & Steyerberg, The Integrated Calibration Index (Stat Med 2019)

name: Hosmer–Lemeshow and Spiegelhalter tests
short: Classical hypothesis tests for calibration. Widely used, widely criticised.
formal: HL: chi-square statistic over g deciles of predicted risk; Spiegelhalter: z-test based on the Brier score decomposition
plain: Hosmer–Lemeshow depends arbitrarily on the number of groups, has poor power in small samples and rejects everything in large ones, and returns a p-value rather than a magnitude. Modern guidance is to prefer the calibration curve with slope, intercept and ICI. Included because you will meet it in the clinical literature and in reviewer comments.
watchOut: A non-significant p-value is not evidence of calibration; it is often just low power.
Sensitive to the number of groups. Generally discouraged in current guidance.

code.snippet:
library(ResourceSelection)
hoslem.test(y, p_hat, g = 10)

refs.cite: Hosmer & Lemeshow (1980)
Van Calster et al., Calibration: the Achilles heel of predictive analytics (BMC Med 2019)

name: PIT histogram & regression reliability diagram
short: Transform each observation through its own predicted CDF; the result should be uniform.
formal: PIT_i = F̂_{x_i}(y_i);  plot the empirical CDF of PIT against the diagonal;  MACE = mean |observed coverage − expected| over quantile levels
plain: The workhorse diagnostic for quantile calibration. The shape of the histogram tells you the failure mode directly: U-shaped means overconfident (intervals too narrow), hump-shaped means underconfident, sloped means biased. The area between the empirical and ideal curves is the usual scalar summary.
watchOut: Marginal only. A perfect PIT histogram is compatible with severe input-dependent miscalibration.
Discrete outcomes need a randomised PIT.

code.snippet:
import uncertainty_toolbox as uct
uct.mean_absolute_calibration_error(pred_mean, pred_std, y)
uct.viz.plot_calibration(pred_mean, pred_std, y)

from netcal.presentation import ReliabilityRegression
ReliabilityRegression(quantiles=11).plot((mu, sigma), y)

refs.cite: Kuleshov, Fenner & Ermon (ICML 2018)
Chung et al., Uncertainty Toolbox (2021)

name: PICP / coverage and interval width
short: What fraction of test points fall inside the nominal interval, and how wide the interval is.
formal: PICP = (1/n) Σ 1{ y_i ∈ [l_i, u_i] };  MPIW = mean(u_i − l_i)
plain: The single-level version of the PIT check, and the natural metric when the deliverable is an interval. Meaningless without the width: an infinitely wide interval has perfect coverage. Report the pair, or a coverage curve over several levels.
watchOut: Never report coverage without width.
Coverage at one level says nothing about the rest of the distribution.

code.snippet:
from netcal.regression import PICP
PICP().measure((mu, sigma), y, q=0.9)
from mapie.metrics import regression_coverage_score, regression_mean_width_score

refs.cite: Pearce et al., High-quality prediction intervals (ICML 2018)

name: ENCE and UCE
short: Bin by predicted standard deviation and compare it with the observed RMSE in each bin.
formal: ENCE = (1/B) Σ_b | RMV(b) − RMSE(b) | / RMV(b),   RMV = root mean predicted variance
plain: The standard estimator for variance calibration, aimed at models that output a mean and a variance. Normalising by the predicted variance makes bins with different uncertainty scales comparable, which is the point. Usually reported with the coefficient of variation, which measures whether the model produces any spread of uncertainties at all.
watchOut: Bin-count dependent, like every binned metric.
Not comparable across datasets with different target scales unless you say what normalisation you used.
Pair with the coefficient of variation: a model that predicts one constant σ can score well.

code.snippet:
from netcal.metrics import ENCE
ENCE(bins=10).measure((mu, sigma), y)

import uncertainty_toolbox as uct
uct.root_mean_squared_calibration_error(pred_mean, pred_std, y)

refs.cite: Levi et al. (Sensors 2022)
Laves et al. (MIDL 2020)

name: CRPS and pinball loss
short: Proper scoring rules for full predictive distributions and for individual quantiles.
formal: CRPS(F, y) = ∫ ( F(z) − 1{z ≥ y} )² dz;   pinball_τ(q, y) = (τ − 1{y < q})(y − q)
plain: The regression counterparts of the Brier score. CRPS decomposes into calibration (reliability) and sharpness terms just as Brier does, and pinball loss is the objective that produces calibrated quantiles when minimised. Report one of these alongside any coverage number so that trivially wide intervals are penalised.
watchOut: A good CRPS does not imply calibration; use the decomposition or a separate PIT check.
Scale-dependent, so normalise before comparing across datasets.

code.snippet:
import scoringrules as sr
sr.crps_normal(mu, sigma, y)

library(scoringutils)
score(forecast_data)

refs.cite: Gneiting & Raftery (JASA 2007)
Hersbach, Decomposition of the CRPS (2000)

name: Group / multicalibration error
short: Calibration error computed within groups, then aggregated by max (worst group) or by the group-conditional squared error.
formal: gASCE(f, g) = E[ Δ²(f) | g(X)=1 ],  with Δ = E[Y − f(X) | level set ∩ group];   MCE(C, f) = max_{c ∈ C} | E[(Y − f(X)) c(X)] |
plain: How multi-group notions are actually measured. For named groups it is per-group ECE plus a max. For a rich class it is the maximum correlation between the residual and any group indicator, which is exactly what the multicalibration post-processing algorithm searches over. The regression analogue samples random slices and reports the worst.
watchOut: Worst-group estimates are biased upward by small groups; report group sizes.
Searching over a rich class on the same data you evaluate on overfits; hold out a split.

code.snippet:
import uncertainty_toolbox as uct
uct.adversarial_group_calibration(pred_mean, pred_std, y)

from fairlearn.metrics import MetricFrame
MetricFrame(metrics=ece_fn, y_true=y, y_pred=p, sensitive_features=g)

refs.cite: Hébert-Johnson et al. (ICML 2018)
Luo et al., Local calibration: metrics and recalibration (UAI 2022)

name: Detection ECE (D-ECE)
short: ECE computed over a joint binning of confidence and box geometry.
formal: D-ECE = Σ_b (n_b/n) | precision(b) − confidence(b) |, with bins over (score, cx, cy, w, h)
plain: The detection-specific estimator. Because the bins are multidimensional, occupancy drops fast as you add box dimensions, so in practice people use two or three dimensions or move to a KDE estimator. Requires you to fix an IoU matching threshold first, and the result depends on it.
watchOut: Curse of dimensionality in the binning; state which box features you conditioned on.
Depends on the IoU threshold and on how unmatched detections are handled.

code.snippet:
from netcal.metrics import ECE
ece = ECE(bins=[15, 5, 5], detection=True)
ece.measure(np.stack([score, cx, cy], axis=1), matched)

refs.cite: Küppers et al., Multivariate confidence calibration for object detection (CVPR-W 2020)
Popordanoska et al. (WACV 2024)

name: Platt scaling
short: Fit a one-dimensional logistic regression from the score to the label on a held-out set.
formal: p̂_cal = σ( a · s(x) + b ),  a and b fitted by maximum likelihood
plain: Two parameters, works with a few hundred held-out points, and is the right default when the validation set is small. Its parametric form assumes the miscalibration is a sigmoid distortion, which fits SVM-style scores well and heavily overconfident deep-network probabilities less well.
watchOut: Cannot fix non-sigmoidal distortions.
Fit on a held-out split, never on the training set.

code.snippet:
from sklearn.calibration import CalibratedClassifierCV
CalibratedClassifierCV(clf, method='sigmoid', cv='prefit').fit(X_val, y_val)

from netcal.scaling import LogisticCalibration
LogisticCalibration().fit(conf_val, y_val).transform(conf_test)

refs.cite: Platt (1999)
Niculescu-Mizil & Caruana (ICML 2005)

name: Isotonic regression
short: Fit the best monotone non-decreasing mapping from score to probability.
formal: min Σ (y_i − g(s_i))²  subject to g non-decreasing;  solved by pool-adjacent-violators
plain: Flexible and assumption-light apart from monotonicity, and the standard strong baseline. It overfits on small validation sets and produces a step function, which means it outputs a small number of distinct probability values. Also the engine behind quantile recalibration in regression.
watchOut: Needs more held-out data than Platt scaling; a common rule of thumb is a thousand or more points.
Piecewise-constant output can be a problem downstream if you need distinct scores for ranking.
Applied one-vs-rest in multiclass, the outputs no longer sum to one; renormalise.

code.snippet:
from sklearn.calibration import CalibratedClassifierCV
CalibratedClassifierCV(clf, method='isotonic', cv='prefit').fit(X_val, y_val)

from netcal.binning import IsotonicRegression
IsotonicRegression().fit(conf_val, y_val).transform(conf_test)

refs.cite: Zadrozny & Elkan (KDD 2002)

name: Histogram binning & scaling-binning
short: Replace each score with the empirical frequency in its bin. Scaling-binning first fits a parametric function, then bins its output.
formal: p̂_cal(x) = mean of y over the bin containing s(x)
plain: The simplest calibrator, and the one whose calibration error you can actually verify, which is the argument for scaling-binning: fitting a smooth function first and binning its outputs afterwards keeps the sample efficiency of the parametric fit while making the result measurable. Bayesian variants (BBQ, ENIR) average over binning schemes.
watchOut: Output is coarse: at most one distinct probability per bin.
Plain histogram binning is sample-hungry; scaling-binning is the better default.

code.snippet:
import calibration as cal
calibrator = cal.PlattBinnerMarginalCalibrator(len(probs_val), num_bins=10)
calibrator.train_calibration(probs_val, y_val)
cal_probs = calibrator.calibrate(probs_test)
from netcal.binning import HistogramBinning, BBQ, ENIR

refs.cite: Zadrozny & Elkan (ICML 2001)
Kumar, Liang & Ma (NeurIPS 2019)

name: Beta calibration
short: A three-parameter family derived from Beta likelihoods, strictly more flexible than Platt scaling.
formal: p̂_cal = σ( a·log s − b·log(1−s) + c )
plain: Fixes a specific defect of Platt scaling: the sigmoid family cannot represent the identity map, so applying it to an already-calibrated model makes it worse. The Beta family contains the identity, handles asymmetric distortions, and still fits from a few hundred points.
watchOut: Binary only; use the Dirichlet generalisation for multiclass.
Requires scores strictly inside (0,1); clip first.

code.snippet:
from netcal.scaling import BetaCalibration
BetaCalibration().fit(conf_val, y_val).transform(conf_test)
from betacal import BetaCalibration

refs.cite: Kull, Silva Filho & Flach, Beta calibration (AISTATS 2017)

name: Temperature scaling
short: Divide all logits by one scalar T, fitted by minimising NLL on a validation set.
formal: p̂_cal = softmax( z / T ),  T > 0 fitted on held-out data
plain: One parameter, preserves the argmax so accuracy is untouched, needs very little data, and works remarkably well for confidence calibration of deep networks. It is also structurally incapable of doing more: a single temperature cannot change the relative ordering within the vector, so it does little for class-wise or canonical calibration.
watchOut: Improves top-label ECE while leaving class-wise miscalibration largely intact.
Degrades under distribution shift; a temperature fitted in-distribution is wrong out of it.
Fitting on the training set gives T ≈ 1 and does nothing.

code.snippet:
from netcal.scaling import TemperatureScaling
ts = TemperatureScaling().fit(logits_val, y_val)
probs = ts.transform(logits_test)

from torch_uncertainty.post_processing import TemperatureScaler
scaler = TemperatureScaler(model); scaler.fit(val_loader)

refs.cite: Guo et al. (ICML 2017)
Ovadia et al., Can you trust your model's uncertainty? (NeurIPS 2019)

name: Vector and matrix scaling
short: An affine transform of the logit vector: a per-class scale (vector) or a full matrix.
formal: p̂_cal = softmax( W z + b ),  W diagonal (vector) or full (matrix)
plain: More expressive than a single temperature, so it can move class-wise calibration, at the cost of K or K² parameters. Matrix scaling overfits badly for large K unless regularised, which is what the ODIR variant of Dirichlet calibration addresses.
watchOut: Matrix scaling needs regularisation for K beyond a few dozen.
Does not preserve the argmax, so accuracy can change.

code.snippet:
from netcal.scaling import LogisticCalibration
LogisticCalibration(detection=False).fit(logits_val, y_val)

refs.cite: Guo et al. (ICML 2017)

name: Dirichlet calibration
short: The multiclass generalisation of beta calibration: a linear map on log-probabilities with off-diagonal regularisation.
formal: p̂_cal = softmax( W · log p̂ + b ),  W regularised toward diagonal (ODIR)
plain: The reference method when you care about class-wise rather than just top-label calibration, and the paper that popularised the confidence / class-wise / canonical distinction in the first place. ODIR regularisation is what makes it usable when K is large.
watchOut: Needs a decent validation set and a regularisation sweep.
Reported to generalise poorly to very large K.

code.snippet:
from dirichletcal.calib.fulldirichlet import FullDirichletCalibrator
cal = FullDirichletCalibrator(reg_lambda=1e-3).fit(probs_val, y_val)

refs.cite: Kull et al., Beyond temperature scaling (NeurIPS 2019)

name: Spline calibration
short: Fit a smooth cubic spline to the empirical calibration function instead of binning or stepping.
formal: p̂_cal = g(s),  g a fitted natural cubic spline of the recalibration curve
plain: Gives a continuous, differentiable recalibration map, which avoids both the step-function artefacts of isotonic regression and the rigidity of a two-parameter sigmoid. A good default when you have a moderate validation set and want smooth outputs.
watchOut: Not monotone by construction unless you constrain it.
Knot placement is a hyperparameter.

code.snippet: # see the authors' repo for the spline calibration code

refs.cite: Gupta et al., Calibration of neural networks using splines (ICLR 2021)

name: Top-label histogram binning
short: Run a separate binary calibrator on the confidence values within each predicted class.
formal: For each predicted label k, fit a binary calibrator on { (max p̂(x), 1{y = k}) : ĉ(x) = k }
plain: The direct algorithm for top-label calibration: reduce to one binary problem per predicted class and solve each with histogram binning, which has distribution-free finite-sample guarantees.
watchOut: Rare predicted classes get few calibration points; the paper discusses the sample-size condition.

code.snippet: # reference implementation accompanying the ICLR 2022 paper

refs.cite: Gupta & Ramdas (ICLR 2022)

name: Multicalibration post-processing
short: Iteratively find the group with the largest residual correlation and patch the predictions on it. Repeat until no group violates.
formal: While ∃ g ∈ C with |E[(Y − f)·g]| > α:  update f on the level sets of g by the observed residual
plain: A boosting loop over an auditing oracle. It converges in a bounded number of steps, works as a black-box post-process, and does not hurt accuracy. The practical question is what class C you audit over: named attributes, a decision tree family, or, for LLMs, functions of the hidden state.
watchOut: Needs a held-out audit set separate from the evaluation set, or the guarantee is optimistic.
The strength of the guarantee is exactly the richness of C; state it.

code.snippet:
library(mcboost)
mc <- MCBoost$new(auditor_fitter = 'TreeAuditorFitter')
mc$multicalibrate(X_val, y_val)
# reference implementation from Detommaso et al. 2024

refs.cite: Hébert-Johnson et al. (ICML 2018)
Pfisterer et al., mcboost (JOSS 2021)

name: Decision calibration algorithm
short: Iteratively correct the prediction vector until no decision rule in the target class can detect a discrepancy.
formal: Alternate: find the worst-case decision rule in L; patch the predictions on the induced partition
plain: Same boosting shape as multicalibration, but the auditing class is a set of decision rules rather than a set of groups. Yields guarantees phrased directly in terms of downstream loss.
watchOut: Guarantees hold only for the specified decision class.
Research-grade tooling.

code.snippet: # see the authors' repo accompanying the NeurIPS 2021 paper

refs.cite: Zhao et al. (NeurIPS 2021)

name: Quantile recalibration
short: Fit a monotone map on the PIT values so that they become uniform, then compose it with the predicted CDF.
formal: R = isotonic fit of  p ↦ empirical P(PIT ≤ p);   F̂_cal = R ∘ F̂
plain: The standard post-hoc fix for quantile calibration in regression: reduce to a one-dimensional binary calibration problem on the PIT values and solve it with isotonic regression. Cheap, model-agnostic, and it targets exactly the marginal notion, no more.
watchOut: Only achieves marginal calibration; input-dependent errors survive.
The recalibrated CDF is a step function with no closed form.

code.snippet:
import uncertainty_toolbox as uct
recal = uct.recalibration.iso_recal(exp_props, obs_props)

from netcal.regression import IsotonicRegression
IsotonicRegression().fit((mu_val, sigma_val), y_val)

refs.cite: Kuleshov, Fenner & Ermon (ICML 2018)

name: GP-Beta
short: A Gaussian-process Beta calibration map that conditions on the predicted distribution rather than only on the quantile level.
formal: Beta calibration map with parameters generated by a GP over the predicted distribution's features
plain: The method proposed alongside the definition of distribution calibration for regression. Because the recalibration map varies with the predicted distribution, it can fix input-dependent miscalibration that a single monotone PIT transform cannot.
watchOut: GP inference cost; needs a reasonable validation set.
Distribution calibration is not exactly attainable, so treat the output as an improvement, not a guarantee.

code.snippet:
from netcal.regression import GPBeta
GPBeta().fit((mu_val, sigma_val), y_val).transform((mu_test, sigma_test))

refs.cite: Song, Diethe, Kull & Flach (ICML 2019)

name: Variance (sigma) scaling
short: Multiply the predicted variance by one fitted scalar.
formal: σ̂²_cal = s · σ̂²,  s fitted by minimising NLL or ENCE on validation data
plain: The regression counterpart of temperature scaling, and the natural companion to variance calibration. One parameter, preserves the mean prediction, fixes the common case of uniformly overconfident error bars, and cannot fix anything input-dependent.
watchOut: Only rescales; if the shape of the uncertainty is wrong, this will not help.
Fit on held-out data, and check ENCE before and after.

code.snippet:
from netcal.regression import VarianceScaling
VarianceScaling().fit((mu_val, sigma_val), y_val)

refs.cite: Levi et al. (Sensors 2022)
Laves et al. (MIDL 2020)

name: Conformal / conformalized quantile regression
short: Adjust intervals or prediction sets using held-out residual quantiles to obtain distribution-free marginal coverage.
formal: C_α(x) = [ q̂_lo(x) − Q_{1−α}(E), q̂_hi(x) + Q_{1−α}(E) ],  E the conformity scores on the held-out split
plain: Delivers coverage, not calibration, but sits in the same pipeline slot and is often the right tool when what you need is a guaranteed-validity interval rather than a probability. Adaptive variants track drift in an online setting.
watchOut: Marginal coverage only; conditional coverage is not guaranteed.
Requires exchangeability, which fails under drift unless you use an adaptive variant.

code.snippet:
from mapie.regression import MapieQuantileRegressor
MapieQuantileRegressor(estimator, alpha=0.1).fit(X, y)
from crepes import WrapRegressor

refs.cite: Romano, Patterson & Candès, Conformalized quantile regression (NeurIPS 2019)
Angelopoulos & Bates (2021)

name: Online / streaming recalibration
short: Update the recalibration map as data arrives, with no i.i.d. assumption.
formal: Online gradient or quantile-tracking updates to the recalibrator, with a no-regret guarantee
plain: What you need when the validation set does not stay valid. Adaptive conformal inference is the best-tooled instance; the game-theoretic calibration literature provides the underlying guarantees for arbitrary sequences.
watchOut: Tracking speed versus stability is a real tradeoff; the step size is a deployment decision.
Guarantees are asymptotic or regret-based, not finite-sample per-step.

code.snippet: from mapie.regression import MapieTimeSeriesRegressor  # ACI-style updates

refs.cite: Gibbs & Candès (NeurIPS 2021)
Foster & Vohra (Biometrika 1998)

name: Focal loss
short: A training loss that down-weights easy examples and, as a side effect, reduces overconfidence.
formal: L = −(1 − p̂_y)^γ log p̂_y
plain: Trains models that are better calibrated out of the box, by implicitly regularising the predicted distribution toward higher entropy. Usually combined with temperature scaling afterwards rather than replacing it.
watchOut: γ is a hyperparameter and interacts with the rest of the recipe.
Can under-confidence the model if overdone.

code.snippet: # Mukhoti et al. focal calibration repo

refs.cite: Mukhoti et al., Calibrating deep neural networks using focal loss (NeurIPS 2020)

name: Label smoothing
short: Train against slightly softened one-hot targets.
formal: y_smooth = (1 − ε)·e_y + ε/K
plain: A one-line change that reduces overconfidence and often improves ECE. It also compresses the logit geometry, which can hurt distillation and can make the model uniformly under-confident.
watchOut: Interacts badly with knowledge distillation.
Improves top-label ECE without necessarily improving class-wise calibration.

code.snippet: torch.nn.CrossEntropyLoss(label_smoothing=0.1)

refs.cite: Müller, Kornblith & Hinton, When does label smoothing help? (NeurIPS 2019)

name: Calibration-aware training objectives
short: Add a differentiable calibration penalty to the training loss.
formal: L = CE + λ · CalibrationPenalty(p̂, y),  the penalty being MMCE, a soft-binned ECE, or a KDE estimator
plain: Trains for calibration directly rather than patching it afterwards. Kernel-based penalties are the natural choice because they are differentiable and unbiased; KDE-based canonical estimators can be used the same way, which is one of the few routes to canonical calibration in training.
watchOut: λ trades calibration against accuracy; sweep it.
In-training calibration does not survive distribution shift any better than post-hoc calibration.

code.snippet:
from ece_kde import get_ece_kde
loss = ce + lam * get_ece_kde(probs, labels, bw, p=1, mc_type='canonical')

refs.cite: Kumar, Sarawagi & Jain (ICML 2018)
Karandikar et al., Soft calibration objectives (NeurIPS 2021)
Popordanoska et al. (NeurIPS 2022)

name: Ensembles and Bayesian approximations
short: Average several predictive distributions. Usually improves calibration, especially under shift.
formal: p̂_ens = (1/M) Σ_m p̂_m
plain: The most reliable general-purpose improvement, and the one that holds up best when the test distribution moves, which is exactly where a fitted temperature stops working. Expensive at train and inference time; cheaper approximations trade some of the benefit away.
watchOut: Not a substitute for recalibration; ensembles can still be miscalibrated, often under-confident after averaging.
Diversity is what buys the improvement; identical members buy nothing.

la = Laplace(model, 'classification'); la.fit(train_loader)

refs.cite: Lakshminarayanan et al., Deep ensembles (NeurIPS 2017)
Ovadia et al. (NeurIPS 2019)

name: Quantile / pinball training
short: Train the model to output quantiles directly by minimising the pinball loss, optionally with an explicit calibration term.
formal: L = Σ_τ pinball_τ( q̂_τ(x), y )  ( + λ · calibration penalty )
plain: Produces quantile-calibrated predictions by construction in the population limit, without assuming a parametric predictive distribution. Later work adds explicit terms to trade calibration against sharpness, or against individual-calibration surrogates.
watchOut: Independently trained quantiles can cross; sort or constrain them.
Finite-sample calibration is not guaranteed; recalibrate afterwards.

code.snippet:
from sklearn.ensemble import GradientBoostingRegressor
GradientBoostingRegressor(loss='quantile', alpha=0.9)
import uncertainty_toolbox as uct  # calibration-sharpness losses
